name: The Approved Tool List
title: The Approved Tool List
answer: An approved tool list is a written district record of which AI tools staff and students may use, together with the rules that apply to each one. It matters because it removes the safety decision from individual teachers and gives the district a clear way to reject tools that have not been reviewed. The list only works when a short, repeatable review and a simple request process keep the approved path the easiest one to follow.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The approved tool list is a single written document that names the AI tools a district permits and the conditions attached to each. It serves two purposes at once, showing teachers which tools are safe to use with student information and giving the district a formal way to decline tools that have not been checked. Without such a list, each teacher ends up making that judgment alone, which is the situation the FTC advises against. The idea solves the problem of scattered, unreviewed tool choices by placing the decision at the district level. It also creates a record that the district can point to when explaining what is and is not allowed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A tool earns a place on the list only after a short review that can be repeated the same way each time. The reviewer checks the age rules, reads the privacy terms, confirms whether a signed data privacy agreement is in place, and tries the tool on a task similar to what teachers would actually assign. Figure 3.3 sets out these steps. The review does not have to stretch over months, but it does need a named owner, usually the technology director, and a written record of the decision. The list also needs a front door for requests, so teachers who find new tools can submit a simple form, receive a promised response time, and get a clear answer of approved, approved with limits, or not approved. The text does not give separate grade band guidance.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or finding beyond the reference to Figure 3.3, which lays out the review steps rather than reporting research results. The only external support named is the FTC's advice against leaving tool choice to each teacher. Otherwise the idea rests on practice and on the district's own review process rather than on research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The list is only as strong as its review and its record keeping, so a named owner and a documented decision are treated as necessary rather than optional. The text warns that without a request process teachers may work around the list, which is why a simple form, a promised response time, and a clear answer of approved, approved with limits, or not approved are part of the design. The judgment about age rules, privacy terms, and data privacy agreements stays with the people conducting the review, not with the tool. The goal is to make the approved path the easiest path, which keeps the decision with the district while still leaving room for teachers to bring forward good new tools.
